who: a county in Kentucky named for a French royal house
why: Corn whiskey barrelled and shipped from that county took its name.
mean: American whiskey distilled mainly from corn and aged in charred oak
story: Barrels of corn whiskey floated down the Ohio and Mississippi from one Kentucky county, whose name was stencilled on the staves. By the time they reached New Orleans the oak had mellowed the spirit, and buyers asked for it by the county on the barrel.

who: a town in Belgium
why: The thick woollen cloth used for the bags was woven there.
mean: A cylindrical canvas bag closed with a drawstring
story: A Belgian town wove a thick coarse wool that soldiers and sailors trusted to keep out weather. Coats and kitbags cut from it carried the town's name across every navy in Europe, and the bag kept the name long after the cloth changed.

who: an American ice-rink owner and inventor (1901-1988)
why: He built the first machine that resurfaces an ice rink in one pass.
mean: A machine that shaves and resurfaces ice
story: Resurfacing a rink took five men over an hour. A rink owner in California spent nine years bolting a shaving blade, a water tank and a squeegee onto an army surplus chassis until one driver could do it in ten minutes. His name is now on the machine everywhere.

who: the daughter of an Austrian car dealer (1889-1929)
why: Her father entered cars under her name, and the maker adopted it.
mean: A German luxury car marque
story: An Austrian businessman raced Daimler cars under his young daughter's name because a foreign entrant needed a pseudonym. The cars won, dealers demanded that model by that name, and the factory quietly made a ten-year-old girl's name its own.

who: the French officer who founded Detroit in 1701
why: The Detroit carmaker took the city founder's name and coat of arms.
mean: An American luxury car; anything of the highest quality
story: A French officer built a fort on a narrow strait and called it the place of the strait, which became Detroit. Two centuries later a carmaker in that city borrowed his name and his family crest, and the word came to mean the best of anything.

who: a Swiss racing driver and engineer (1878-1941)
why: He co-founded the car company that carries his surname.
mean: An American car marque
story: A Swiss racing driver went into partnership with an ousted car executive, lending his famous name to a new company. He fell out with his partner over building cheap cars, sold his shares early, and watched his surname become one of the biggest in America.

who: an American frontiersman who died at the Alamo (1796-1836)
why: His fighting knife became famous after a sandbar brawl in 1827.
mean: A large single-edged sheath knife with a clipped point
story: A frontiersman was shot and stabbed in a duel-turned-brawl on a Mississippi sandbar and still killed two men with a heavy butcher's knife. Newspapers described the blade in detail, smiths were flooded with orders, and the knife took his name.

who: a fortified city in south-west France
why: The blade that fits a musket muzzle was first made or first used there.
mean: A blade fixed to the muzzle of a rifle
story: The story goes that soldiers besieged in a French border city ran out of powder and jammed their hunting knives into their musket barrels. Whether or not that happened, the city's forges made the blades, and its name went onto them.

who: the island nation
why: European makers copied Japanese lacquerwork and called the hard glossy black finish by the country's name.
mean: A hard glossy black lacquer finish
story: Lacquered boxes arriving from East Asia in the 1600s astonished Europe with a black finish nothing local could match. Workshops in England and France tried to copy it, sold the results as the country's own name, and turned a nation into a verb.

who: one of the Channel Islands
why: The island's fishermen wore a close-knit woollen jumper that took its name.
mean: A close-fitting knitted woollen jumper; also a breed of dairy cow
story: Fishermen on a small Channel Island knitted jumpers so tightly that seawater ran off them. Naval crews adopted the pattern, Australian footballers borrowed the word for their shirts, and the island's dairy cattle carried the same name to farms worldwide.

who: a valley in southern Scotland
why: The heavy draught horse was bred by farmers along that valley.
mean: A very large draught horse with feathered legs
story: Farmers in one Scottish river valley crossed local mares with imported Flemish stallions to get a horse that could haul coal and plough heavy clay. The breed grew to a tonne, kept its white feathered legs, and carried the valley's name to the world.

who: a Greek city and port
why: The tiny dried grapes were shipped from there as raisins of Corinth.
mean: A small dried grape used in baking
story: Medieval traders bought tiny seedless dried grapes at a Greek port and sold them in England as raisins of that city. The phrase wore down over centuries until only a mangled version of the city's name was left on the packet.

who: an ancient port in the Levant, now Ashkelon
why: Crusaders brought the small clustered onion home and named it after the port.
mean: A small mild onion that grows in clusters
story: Returning crusaders brought back a small onion that grew in clusters and tasted milder than the ones at home. They said it came from one Levantine port, called it the onion of that place, and French cooks wore the phrase down to a single word.

who: a river in ancient Colchis, on the Black Sea
why: Greeks said the bird came from the banks of that river.
mean: A long-tailed game bird with bright plumage
story: Greek sailors returning from the Black Sea brought back a spectacular long-tailed bird and said it lived along one particular river. They called it the bird of the Phasis, and every European language still carries a worn-down version of that river's name.

who: the Italian word for sunflower, misheard as a city name
why: The plant is a sunflower relative, and girasole was corrupted into a holy city's name.
mean: A knobbly edible tuber from a sunflower relative
story: The knobbly tuber is a North American sunflower and has never grown near the Middle East. Italians called the plant girasole, turning to the sun; English ears heard a famous city in that word, and the wrong name has stuck for four hundred years.

who: the Dutch region
why: The butter-and-egg sauce was said to imitate a Dutch style of cooking.
mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter and lemon
story: French cooks named several sauces after foreign countries to suggest a style rather than an origin. This one, whisked from yolks and warm butter until it thickens, was labelled Dutch, possibly because the Netherlands supplied the butter.

who: a region in the French Pyrenees
why: The sauce was named at a restaurant honouring a king born in that region.
mean: A warm sauce of egg yolk, butter, tarragon and shallot
story: A chef outside Paris invented a herbed butter sauce at a restaurant named for Henry IV, who was born in a Pyrenean region and nicknamed for it. The sauce took the region's name, though nobody there had ever made it.

who: a hilly wine region in Tuscany
why: The red wine comes from vineyards in those hills.
mean: A dry red Italian wine
story: A grand duke drew a boundary round some Tuscan hills in 1716 and declared that only wine from inside it could carry the region's name. It was one of the first protected wine areas anywhere, three centuries before such rules became normal.

who: a wine region north of Lyon in France
why: The light red wine made from gamay grapes there carries the region's name.
mean: A light fruity red wine
story: Growers in a French region north of Lyon make a light red from gamay grapes and release the newest vintage on the third Thursday of November. Bottles race to Paris and beyond overnight, and the region's name goes with every cork.

who: a village in the Maconnais, Burgundy
why: The white grape variety takes the village's name.
mean: A white wine grape, or the wine made from it
story: A small Burgundy village gave its name to a green-skinned grape that turned out to grow almost anywhere, from Champagne to California to Australia. It is now the most planted white wine grape on earth, still carrying one village's name.

who: a wine region in northern Spain
why: The oak-aged red wine of the Ebro valley takes the region's name.
mean: A Spanish red wine aged in oak
story: When disease wrecked French vineyards in the 1800s, Bordeaux winemakers crossed the Pyrenees and taught growers in a northern Spanish valley to age wine in oak barrels. The region kept the technique, and its name now means oak-aged Spanish red.

who: the Greek Muse of epic poetry
why: The steam whistle organ was named for the Muse whose name means beautiful-voiced.
mean: A loud musical instrument of steam whistles
story: An inventor in 1855 mounted a keyboard on a row of steam whistles loud enough to be heard eight miles away. He named it for the Muse of epic poetry, whose name means beautiful-voiced, which anyone who has stood near a circus one may dispute.

who: the brutish human-like creatures in Gulliver's Travels
why: Swift's filthy, violent creatures gave their name to any coarse lout.
mean: A crude, loud, uncultivated person
story: On his last voyage Gulliver meets talking horses ruling over filthy, howling creatures that look uncomfortably like humans. Swift meant it as a mirror. The creatures' name became an insult, and much later a search engine picked it up as a joke.

who: the impossible rule in Joseph Heller's 1961 novel
why: The rule made escape logically impossible, so its name means any such trap.
mean: A problem whose only solution is blocked by the problem itself
story: A bomber pilot could be grounded for insanity, but asking to be grounded proved he was sane enough to fly. Heller's invented regulation was so exact a picture of bureaucratic traps that its number entered the dictionary within a decade.

who: the shrinking official language in Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: Its purpose was to make rebellious thought impossible by deleting words.
mean: Deliberately ambiguous or misleading official language
story: In Orwell's novel the state shrinks the dictionary every year, on the theory that a thought you have no word for cannot be thought at all. The invented language's name is now used for any official wording designed to blur rather than explain.

who: the mental habit demanded by the Party in Nineteen Eighty-Four
why: It meant holding two contradictory beliefs at once and accepting both.
mean: Holding two contradictory beliefs at the same time
story: Orwell's Party required citizens to believe two opposite things at once and to be sincere about both, forgetting the contradiction and then forgetting the forgetting. The coined word escaped the novel and is now used of real politics every week.

who: the acrobatic trickster servant of Italian commedia dell'arte
why: His diamond-patterned costume gave the word for that pattern.
mean: A pattern of coloured diamonds; a comic acrobatic character
story: A masked servant character in Italian street comedy wore a patched costume that hardened over time into neat coloured diamonds. He tumbled, schemed and chased Columbine through two centuries of theatre, and left his name on the pattern itself.

who: the servant clowns of Italian commedia dell'arte
why: The clown who mimicked his master gave his name to anything absurdly comic.
mean: Amusingly unconventional and idiotic
story: In Italian street comedy the servant clowns, named from a dialect form of Giovanni, copied their masters' gestures badly on purpose. English audiences took the troupe's name for the behaviour, and it now describes any cheerfully absurd person.

who: the Greek sun god
why: The gas was detected in the sun's spectrum before it was found on earth.
mean: The lightest inert gas, used to fill balloons
story: During an eclipse in 1868 astronomers saw a yellow line in the sun's spectrum that matched no known element. They named the unknown gas after the Greek sun god. Twenty-seven years passed before anyone found any of it on earth.

who: an English baronet (1657-1727)
why: He imported the plum from France, and the labels were lost in transit.
mean: A small sweet green plum
story: An English baronet imported plum trees from a French monastery, and the labels were lost on the way. His gardener, needing something to call the green ones, combined the colour with his employer's surname, and the plum has answered to it since.

who: a Massachusetts merchant (1779-1860)
why: He distributed the English Williams pear in America under his own name.
mean: A large sweet yellow pear
story: An English variety called the Williams pear was already growing on a Massachusetts farm when a merchant bought the land. Not knowing the name, he propagated and sold it under his own. The same fruit still has two names on two sides of the Atlantic.

who: a Soviet tank sergeant turned weapons designer (1919-2013)
why: He designed the rifle while recovering from wounds in 1942.
mean: A Soviet-designed automatic rifle
story: A wounded Soviet tank sergeant lay in hospital listening to comrades complain that German troops had better automatic weapons. He sketched a design built to work when filled with mud or sand. Over a hundred million have been made, all carrying his name.

who: a German firearms designer (1838-1914)
why: His bolt-action rifle became the pattern copied by most armies.
mean: A German bolt-action rifle or pistol
story: A German designer perfected a bolt action so reliable that armies from Spain to Japan bought or copied it, and hunting rifles still use his locking system a century later. His surname is stamped on more military rifles than almost any other.

who: a German physicist (1858-1947)
why: He found that energy comes in fixed packets set by one small number.
mean: The fixed quantity linking a photon's energy to its frequency
story: A German physicist trying to explain the colour of hot glowing objects found the maths only worked if energy came in indivisible packets. He called the idea a desperate act. It founded quantum theory, and the tiny number in it carries his name.

who: a Danish physicist (1885-1962)
why: He pictured electrons in fixed orbits that could only jump between set levels.
mean: A picture of the atom with electrons in fixed energy orbits
story: A Danish physicist proposed that electrons could only sit in certain orbits and jumped between them by swallowing or spitting out exact packets of light. It explained hydrogen's spectrum precisely, was wrong in detail, and is still the first atom every student draws.

who: a French physicist (1819-1868)
why: He hung a heavy pendulum in the Pantheon to show the earth turning beneath it.
mean: A long free-swinging pendulum that demonstrates the earth's rotation
story: In 1851 a French physicist hung a sixty-seven-metre wire from the dome of the Pantheon with a heavy iron ball on the end. As it swung, its path slowly rotated. Paris could watch the planet turning for the first time, in a public hall.

who: an Italian physicist and priest (1746-1822)
why: He showed that fluid speeds up and its pressure drops in a narrowing pipe.
mean: The drop in pressure when a fluid speeds through a narrowing
story: An Italian priest and physicist showed that squeezing a pipe makes the fluid inside run faster and press outwards less. Carburettors, atomisers, aircraft instruments and hospital suction all use the trick, and all carry his name for it.

who: an Irish-born engineer (1842-1912)
why: He found a single number that predicts whether flow will be smooth or turbulent.
mean: A number predicting whether a flow will be smooth or turbulent
story: An engineer injected a thread of dye into water flowing down a glass pipe. Below a certain speed the thread stayed straight; above it, the dye burst into swirls. He reduced the whole question to one dimensionless ratio that now bears his name.

who: a Japanese-American meteorologist (1920-1998)
why: He rated tornado strength by the damage left behind.
mean: A scale rating tornado strength by damage
story: A meteorologist who had surveyed the blast damage at Nagasaki applied the same eye to tornado wreckage, working backwards from broken buildings to wind speed. His damage-based scale, from a snapped branch to a house swept clean off its slab, still rates every twister.

who: an English mathematician (1685-1731)
why: He showed how to rebuild a function from its derivatives at a single point.
mean: An infinite sum that reproduces a function from its derivatives at one point
story: An English mathematician showed that if you know a curve's height, slope, curvature and every higher rate of change at just one point, you can rebuild the entire curve as an endless sum. Almost all of numerical computing rests on that trick.

who: a German mathematician (1862-1943)
why: He generalised ordinary geometry to spaces with infinitely many dimensions.
mean: A complete space with infinitely many dimensions and a notion of angle
story: A German mathematician extended ordinary distance and angle into spaces with endlessly many directions. It sounded like pure abstraction until quantum mechanics arrived and turned out to need exactly that geometry to describe the state of a particle.

who: a German mathematician (1804-1851)
why: He studied the matrix of partial derivatives that tells how a transformation stretches space.
mean: The matrix of partial derivatives of a vector function
story: A German mathematician studied the grid of partial derivatives that says how much a change of coordinates stretches or twists each direction. Its determinant is the factor by which volume changes, which is why it appears in every multiple integral.

who: a German mathematician (1811-1874)
why: He studied the square array of second derivatives that describes curvature.
mean: The square matrix of second partial derivatives of a function
story: A German mathematician assembled all the second derivatives of a function into one square array. Its signs tell you whether a flat point is a peak, a valley or a saddle, which is why every optimisation algorithm reaches for it.

who: a plateau town in the Veneto, northern Italy
why: The cow's-milk cheese has been made on that plateau for centuries.
mean: A firm Italian cow's-milk cheese
story: Shepherds on a high plateau in northern Italy once made this cheese from sheep's milk. When cattle replaced the flocks the recipe changed but the name did not, and European law now protects it for that plateau alone.

who: a small town in Wisconsin
why: A cheesemaker's son invented the washed-curd cheese there in 1885.
mean: A mild orange American cheese with a springy texture
story: A Wisconsin cheesemaker's teenage son washed the curds in cold water instead of letting them cook dry, and got a softer, milder, moister cheese than cheddar. It was the first cheese invented in America, and it took the little town's name.

who: an experimental farm outside Copenhagen
why: A Danish cheesemaker developed the cheese at that farm in the 1800s.
mean: A semi-soft Danish cheese with small holes
story: A Danish woman toured European dairies, came home to an experimental farm outside Copenhagen, and worked out a semi-soft cheese full of tiny irregular holes. The farm's name went onto it, and Denmark's best-known cheese was born on a research plot.

who: the northern Italian city
why: The city's cooks breadcrumb and fry veal, and saffron their risotto.
mean: Coated in breadcrumbs and fried, in the style of one Italian city
story: A northern Italian city gave its name to two very different dishes: a veal cutlet beaten thin, breadcrumbed and fried in butter, and a risotto turned gold with saffron. Vienna's schnitzel is very probably the same cutlet under another flag.

who: a French city famous for its cooking
why: Dishes finished with sliced onions are named for the city's style.
mean: Cooked with sliced onions, in the style of one French city
story: One French city is so serious about food that its small restaurants have their own name, bouchons. Any dish labelled with the city's adjective on a French menu comes with sliced onions browned in butter, whatever else is on the plate.

who: a sunny region of southern France
why: Dishes with tomato, garlic and olive oil take the region's name.
mean: Cooked with tomato, garlic and olive oil
story: The name of a southern French region on a menu promises the same three things every time: tomato, garlic and olive oil, usually with herbs from the dry hills. The region's Roman name simply meant the province, the first one Rome held outside Italy.

who: the miserly old Venetian merchant of commedia dell'arte
why: His tight leg-covering costume gave its name to trousers.
mean: Wide or tight trousers, depending on the century
story: A stock character in Italian street comedy played a mean old Venetian merchant in tight full-length hose, unusual when other men wore breeches. Audiences named the garment after him, French shortened it, and the word ended up as plain pants.

who: the boastful cowardly soldier of commedia dell'arte
why: His swagger and swift retreat made his name a word for a boastful rogue.
mean: A boastful coward; a roguish clown
story: A stock character in Italian comedy strutted in black with a sword, boasted of battles he had not fought, and ran at the first real threat. His name, from a word meaning skirmish, became the English word for exactly that sort of man.

who: the hypocritical architect in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit
why: He preached morality endlessly while behaving badly, so his name means smug hypocrisy.
mean: Smugly and hypocritically moralising
story: Dickens created an architect who never designed a building, lived off his pupils' work, and lectured everyone he met about virtue while cheating them. His name became the exact English word for moralising that the moraliser has no intention of following.
